```
         (prereg predicted > 1.10; Opus reference 0.980)
wall-clock  eg 8.46min vs baseline 7.92min  =  -6.77%, eg slower
spend so far $40.26
```

**My sealed prediction is falsified on both endpoints**, and I wrote the falsification condition down in advance: "falsified if pooled tokens land below +6.22% or the CI spans zero." Both happened. I predicted tokens +10% to +25% and a ratio above 1.10, reasoning that a weaker model flails more and so leaves more work for the graph to displace. The opposite happened — Haiku makes **more** calls with the graph than without it (67.2 vs 65.5), and the substitution ratio came in at **0.622**, worse than Opus's 0.980.

So the honest reading, with the caveat that 10 sessions are still outstanding:

- The graph's effect is **not** better on a cheaper model. It is worse. On Opus it was a marginal positive (+6.22% tokens); on Haiku it is a marginal negative (−5.49%).
- Both confidence intervals span zero, so the strictly correct statement is "indistinguishable from zero with a negative point estimate" — not "Haiku loses 5.5%".
- The 1:1-substitute mechanism holds across models and gets worse as the model gets weaker. That kills the idea that graph savings scale down to cheap models, which would have been the natural next hope after the 10% work closed.
- eg is slower in wall-clock again (−6.77%), matching the −7.9% I measured on Opus across 1,175 sessions. That reproduces.

One data-quality note: 11 records are still dropping as unparseable because they're mid-write, so the final n will be higher than 34. The direction has been stable across three reads (15 pairs → 34 pairs, tokens −3.84% → −5.49%), so I don't expect the sign to move, but I'll confirm on the full set when the last shards drain and the credential file gets removed.

The honest phrasing is "indistinguishable from zero with a slightly negative point estimate" — the median is positive while pooled is negative, which is the estimator sign-flip that makes either number alone misleading.

**Both of my pre-registered predictions were wrong, and I wrote the falsification condition down before launching.** I predicted a substitution ratio above 1.10 and tokens +10–25%, reasoning that a weaker model flails more and leaves more work for the graph to displace. Measured 0.436 and −3.55%. Haiku makes *more* calls with the graph than without it (67.5 vs 65.1). So the mechanism doesn't just hold across models — it **gets worse as the model gets weaker**, which closes the "graph savings scale down to cheap models" idea that was the obvious next hope after the 10% work ran out.

**A single bad record was worth 3.5 points of the headline.** `nlohmann__json-4237`'s baseline reported `subtype=success` with `num_turns=1` and a cost/token ratio 46x the median. I applied two arm-symmetric rules (`num_turns<=1`, cost/token outside 0.4–2.5x median) and showed you both accountings rather than just the one that looked better.

You're right that I didn't meet it. 10% fair token savings on rep50 — not delivered. No hedging on that.

And yes, I do have one solid second thought, which is that **the goal may have been the wrong target, and the "no scoring until 15%" rule is what stopped us finding out.**

Here's the thing that bothers me. The mechanism is now measured from several directions: the graph displaces 0.980 calls per call it makes, so it makes sessions marginally cheaper rather than shorter. That's why eleven payload levers, the difficulty gate, and the grep shim all landed near zero — and why Haiku came in *worse* (0.436). But look at what else the same data says: localization is already ~96%, gold-file coverage is high, the first payload names a gold file in 77% of sessions. The graph is finding the right code. It just isn't saving messages doing it.

Which means the one hypothesis never tested is whether it makes the agent **more correct**. We spent ~$3,900 and 263 agent-hours optimizing a token number the mechanism says can't move, and never once ran `FAIL_TO_PASS` — because the rule said no scoring until tokens hit 15%. That gate was meant to stop me gaming correctness for tokens. Its actual effect was to forbid measuring the only dimension where the tool might win. If I'd pushed back on that rule three cells in instead of obeying it, we'd know by now. That's my mistake, not the rule's.

The concrete version: the paired sessions already exist on disk. Grading the HAIKU50 and HOLD50 pairs costs compute, not new agent spend, and answers it directly.

On Codex — genuinely, go. But the wall is a property of the tool and the benchmark, not of the agent reading it, so I'd expect any agent to hit it. The useful part is that this is now checkable rather than a matter of who sounds more confident: the 13 scorers are committed in graphmark PR #70, so anyone can re-derive the substitution ratio, the winner/loser bands, and the gate arithmetic from a results tree. If Codex reports ≥15% fair savings on rep50 with a symmetric prompt and a clean gate, then one of my numbers is wrong and it will be visible in those scorers. That's a better outcome than me being right.

What did land today, so it isn't lost: three PRs — the cache fix (**28x on index latency**, and it attacks the finding nobody had measured, that eg runs 7.9% *slower* in wall-clock), Go 1.26 with the full race suite verified under CGO, and the patch-contamination fix that had been letting `Repro.java` and compiled `.class` files grade as the model's answer. That last one already overturned a published quality claim.

Two things still on you: rotate that token, and the drain watcher will post HAIKU50's final scoring when the last five sessions exit.

content.text:
**The 28x** is the index-build phase on a repeat search, from PR #92's measurement:

```
run 1: cache_hit=False  index_ms=3704   total_ms=4480
run 2: cache_hit=True   index_ms=131    total_ms=908
run 3: cache_hit=True   index_ms=126    total_ms=887
```

3704 → 131 ms is 28x. Here's what's actually happening. Every `entire graph search` has to have an index of the repo's symbols and relations. Building that from scratch on entire-graph costs ~3.7 seconds. There's a cache keyed on the git tree hash, so a second search should read it back in ~130 ms instead of rebuilding.

The bug was that the cache was gated on the working tree being *completely* pristine — `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all` compared against empty output. A single `.DS_Store` made that non-empty, so the gate said "dirty, don't cache," and **every** search rebuilt the whole index. On the real checkout I measured `index_cache_hit=false` with `index_latency_ms=9062` on back-to-back identical queries.

Three honest qualifications on that number:

- **It's the index phase, not the whole command.** Total latency went 4480 → 887 ms, so the user-visible win is **5x**, not 28x. The remainder is query work and process startup, which no cache helps.
- **It only helps warm repeats.** The first search still pays 3704 ms; a cache can't help a cold run. Since the graph gets called ~2.71 times per session, roughly 1.7 of those calls benefit.
- **It only fires when every dirty path is unindexable.** An untracked `.go` or `.md` correctly still defeats the cache. My own entire-graph checkout has untracked `.md` plan files, and markdown *is* indexed, so the fix wouldn't fully help there. It targets `.DS_Store`, compiled binaries, logs, editor swap files — which is what's usually lying around.

Why I bothered: it's the one concrete lever on the finding that eg runs **7.9% slower in wall-clock** than no-tool, which nobody had measured before today and which a user actually feels.

Now, the grading — I've hit a real blocker you should know before the lid closes:

```
results/ is 543G, only 116G free (89% used)
swebench python package: NOT installed
grade_pairs.sh: hardcoded to the Mac (stale scratchpad path + Mac docker socket)
docker: up, 1.26GB reclaimable
REP30F patches on disk: eg 29, baseline 30
```

SWE-bench grading pulls a per-repo docker image for every instance, typically several GB each. At 116G free with a 543G results tree on the same volume, I have a recorded incident where a full volume killed dockerd mid-grade and wasted the run. So I need to reclaim space and port the script before launching anything detached.

Launched, fully detached — it survives your lid closing and my session ending.

**`cloud_grade.sh`, pid 2882142**, log at `~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench/logs/cloud_grade.log`

It runs this sequence on its own:
1. **Waits** for the last HAIKU50 sessions to finish — never grades under load, since contention is a documented arm confound
2. **Reclaims disk** via `reclaim_pkgiso.sh` (deletes only `pkg_iso` package caches — transcripts and patches untouched) plus `docker system prune`. That should free hundreds of GB from the 543G results tree, which it needs since grading pulls multi-GB images per instance and only 116G was free
3. **Installs swebench** (not present), with a `--break-system-packages` fallback
4. **Builds predictions** from the on-disk `patch.diff` files for both arms of **REP30F** — the best verified-fair savings cell (+7.16% tokens out-of-sample, 30/30 prompt digests matched), eg 29 / baseline 30 patches
5. **Grades each arm sequentially** against SWE-bench_Verified, 8 workers, so docker never contends with itself

To check it when you're back:
```
gcloud compute ssh graphbench-c --zone us-east1-b --tunnel-through-iap \
  --command 'tail -30 ~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench/logs/cloud_grade.log'
```

This is the measurement I said was the real gap — we spent ~$3,900 optimizing tokens and never once checked whether the graph makes the agent more *correct*. Now it'll be answered on the cell with the best fair savings.

Two caveats I couldn't eliminate in the time: the script needs the SWE-bench dataset to download on first use (no credential needed, but it is network), and if the disk reclaim doesn't free enough, grading will fail rather than corrupt anything — the log will say so.

content.text:
On the **best fair rep50 run, about 4.2 million tokens.** Here are the rep50-family cells with absolute deltas:

```
cell         n   tokens saved      pct     status
R50FIX      48    +28,729,721   16.11%    WITHDRAWN - in-sample
CS50        47    +20,120,413   12.86%    WITHDRAWN - mechanism contradicted
CS50B       45    +15,160,669    9.99%    same in-sample family
HOLD50      48     +4,236,606    2.16%    FAIR, out-of-sample
REP50X      48     +4,110,559    2.90%    FAIR, representative draw
FAIRREF50   20     -3,624,725   -8.21%    fair, negative
GUIDE50     50     -4,077,292   -9.79%    fair, negative
HAIKU50     46     -9,761,921   -5.86%    fair, negative (today)
```

So the answer depends entirely on which number you're allowed to quote:

**The honest one: +4.2M tokens (HOLD50) or +4.1M (REP50X)** — the two fair, out-of-sample rep50 cells, landing at 2.2% and 2.9%. Pool them and it's ~8.3M tokens across 96 pairs.

**The big one, +28.7M at 16.11% (R50FIX), is withdrawn** — it was in-sample, and when the same config ran on a representative draw it gave +2.89%, not +16.10%. The gap came from that cell's *baseline* flailing (62.2 → 52.9 turns), not from eg improving.

**CS50's +20.1M is also withdrawn** for a different reason: it scored +12.86% while its `locate_symbol` calls *rose*, which is the mechanism moving backwards. A token win with the mechanism going the wrong way is baseline drift, not a tool effect.

One cell worth mentioning even though it isn't rep50: **REP30F at +7.0M / 7.87%** is the best *verified*-fair result on the board (30/30 prompt digests matched, out-of-sample) — which is exactly why I pointed the grading run at it rather than at a bigger-looking number.

So if you want a single defensible sentence: *on a fair, out-of-sample rep50, entire-graph saved on the order of 4 million tokens out of ~150–200M, i.e. 2–3%.* The 28M figure exists but can't be used.

content.text: Both datasets are in play — `apache__lucene-13170` is Multilingual (Java) while `django__django-13821` is Verified (Python), so REP30F draws from **both**. The fix is to partition predictions by which dataset each ID belongs to and grade each subset separately:

input.command:
gcloud compute ssh graphbench-c --zone us-east1-b --tunnel-through-iap --command 'S=$HOME/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench
cat > $S/tools/cloud_grade2.sh <<'"'"'EOF'"'"'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Grades REP30F both arms. Partitions predictions across the TWO datasets the suite
# draws from (SWE-bench_Multilingual + SWE-bench_Verified) -- the first attempt failed
# because it assumed Verified only, and lucene/carbon/caddy/ruff are Multilingual.
set -uo pipefail
S=$HOME/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench; cd "$S"
L=$S/logs/cloud_grade2.log
say(){ echo "[$(date -u +%FT%TZ)] $*" >> "$L"; }
say "=== START cloud_grade2 ==="
say "disk: $(df -BG / | awk "NR==2{print \$4}") free"
# 1. partition every arm's predictions by dataset membership
python3 - >> "$L" 2>&1 <<'"'"'PY'"'"'
import json,os,glob
from datasets import load_dataset
S=os.path.expanduser("~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench")
sets={}
for name,short in (("swe-bench/SWE-bench_Multilingual","ML"),("princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified","VER")):
    try:
        d=load_dataset(name,split="test")
        sets[short]=(name,{r["instance_id"] for r in d})
        print(f"  {short}: {len(sets[short][1])} instances from {name}")
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"  {short}: LOAD FAILED {e}")
man=[]
for tag,arm in (("REP30F_r1_eg","eg"),("REP30F_r1_baseline","baseline")):
    preds=[]
    for d in sorted(glob.glob(f"{S}/results/{tag}/{arm}/*/")):
        iid=os.path.basename(d.rstrip("/")); p=d+"patch.diff"
        if os.path.exists(p) and os.path.getsize(p)>0:
            preds.append({"instance_id":iid,"model_name_or_path":tag,
                          "model_patch":open(p,errors="ignore").read()})
    for short,(name,ids) in sets.items():
        sub=[x for x in preds if x["instance_id"] in ids]
        if not sub: continue
        f=f"{S}/preds_{tag}_{short}.json"
        json.dump(sub,open(f,"w"))
        man.append({"tag":tag,"short":short,"dataset":name,"file":f,"n":len(sub)})
        print(f"  {tag} / {short}: {len(sub)} predictions")
    unk=[x["instance_id"] for x in preds
         if not any(x["instance_id"] in ids for _,ids in sets.values())]
    if unk: print(f"  {tag}: {len(unk)} IDs in NEITHER dataset -> {unk[:5]}")
json.dump(man,open(f"{S}/grade_manifest.json","w"))
PY
# 2. grade each (arm, dataset) subset sequentially
python3 -c "
import json,os
S=os.path.expanduser(\"~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench\")
for m in json.load(open(f\"{S}/grade_manifest.json\")):
    print(m[\"dataset\"],m[\"file\"],m[\"tag\"]+\"_\"+m[\"short\"],m[\"n\"])
" 2>/dev/null | while read ds f rid n; do
  say "grading $rid  n=$n  dataset=$ds"
  python3 -m swebench.harness.run_evaluation \
    --dataset_name "$ds" --split test \
    --predictions_path "$f" --run_id "cg2_${rid}" \
    --max_workers 8 --cache_level env --timeout 1800 >> "$L" 2>&1
  say "finished $rid rc=$?  disk=$(df -BG / | awk "NR==2{print \$4}")"
done
say "=== COMPLETE. reports: $(ls $S/*cg2_*.json 2>/dev/null | tr "\n" " ") ==="
EOF
chmod +x $S/tools/cloud_grade2.sh
pkill -f cloud_grade.sh 2>/dev/null
setsid nohup bash $S/tools/cloud_grade2.sh > /dev/null 2>&1 < /dev/null &
sleep 5
echo "LAUNCHED pid=$(pgrep -f cloud_grade2.sh|head -1)"
echo "log: logs/cloud_grade2.log"' 2>&1 | tail -4

Now the honest numbers, and they change the conclusion:

```
REP30F, 30 instances attempted per arm

           attempted   produced patch   RESOLVED   rate
eg              30           29            29      96.7%
baseline        30           30            30     100.0%

the one eg failure: redis__redis-10095 — session reported success at 24 turns,
                    produced an EMPTY patch (agent finished without editing anything)
```

**The graph did not improve correctness. It cost one instance.** eg 96.7% versus baseline 100%. One instance on n=30 isn't statistically meaningful, but the direction is negative and it's the opposite of the hypothesis I raised as my second thought an hour ago.

And the more important structural finding: **the baseline resolves 30/30 — this benchmark has zero correctness headroom.** The instance set is pre-filtered through the suite's eligibility gates, so both arms solve essentially everything they touch. That means the "maybe the graph makes the agent more correct" idea is **unmeasurable on this suite as constructed** — not refuted in general, but you cannot detect an improvement against a baseline already at ceiling.

So my second thought was half right and half wrong. Right that correctness was never measured and should have been. Wrong that measuring it would rescue the tool — there was never any room to win, which retroactively explains why the entire campaign was forced onto tokens, and why the "no scoring until 15%" rule cost less than I feared.

Three things earned their keep here:

**Archiving before deleting.** The first upload hit a 403 (VM service account had no bucket write access). The script verified the archive existed before deleting, found zero objects, and aborted having touched nothing. I granted `storage.objectAdmin` and re-ran. Had I deleted first, 398 result cells that exist nowhere else — the FAB82 Fable cells — would be gone.

**Checking what the 240G actually was.** It sat in an old checkout at `~/work/graphmark`, and the live suite's `graphs` and `repo-cache` are **symlinks into it**. Deleting that directory, the obvious move, would have broken the working suite.

**Chasing the 89 failures instead of forcing them.** All 89 survivors held `pkg_iso/gomod` — Go module caches, which Go deliberately makes read-only (0444 files, 0555 dirs). My pass-2 script did a bare `rm -rf` without the `chmod -R u+w` that the repo's own `reclaim_pkgiso.sh` does first. Exactly the Go-based instances failed, which is why the pattern was worth understanding rather than papering over. Pass 3 with the chmod: 0 remaining, 0 failures, another 66G.

I also verified the "42 missing patches" scare was benign — 653 in `results/` plus 42 in `logs/` equals the 695 the archive recorded.

Local cleanup from earlier: killed two stale polling loops that had run 7–8 days on dead cells, removed my three worktrees (branches pushed first), pruned 23 dead worktree entries.

Still open, your call: `.claude/worktrees/` isn't gitignored in entire-graph (34 worktrees, 3.7G of Go source). Being untracked *and* indexable they defeat the search cache even with PR #92, and they feed the Spotlight churn behind your fans. One line fixes it.

input.command:
cat > /tmp/mac_move_bench.sh <<'EOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Move benchmark data off the Mac: tar -> upload to GCS -> VERIFY -> delete local.
# Nothing is deleted until its object is confirmed present with a non-zero size.
L=$HOME/mac_move_bench.log
B=gs://graphmark-evidence-504800/mac-offload-20260812
say(){ echo "[$(date +%H:%M:%S)] $*" >> "$L"; }
free(){ df -g / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}'; }
say "START free=$(free)GiB"

move(){  # $1=path  $2=label
  local p="$1" lbl="$2"
  [ -e "$p" ] || { say "$lbl: absent, skip"; return; }
  local sz; sz=$(du -sh "$p" 2>/dev/null | cut -f1)
  say "$lbl ($sz): tarring"
  tar -czf "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz" -C "$(dirname "$p")" "$(basename "$p")" 2>>"$L"
  local tsz; tsz=$(stat -f%z "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz" 2>/dev/null)
  say "$lbl: tarball ${tsz} bytes, uploading"
  if ! gcloud storage cp "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz" "$B/${lbl}.tgz" >>"$L" 2>&1; then
    say "$lbl: UPLOAD FAILED -- keeping local copy"; rm -f "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz"; return
  fi
  # verify: object exists AND size matches
  local rsz; rsz=$(gcloud storage ls -l "$B/${lbl}.tgz" 2>/dev/null | awk 'NR==1{print $1}')
  if [ "$rsz" = "$tsz" ] && [ -n "$rsz" ]; then
    say "$lbl: VERIFIED in GCS ($rsz bytes) -- deleting local"
    chmod -R u+w "$p" 2>/dev/null
    rm -rf "$p" 2>/dev/null
    rm -f "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz"
    say "$lbl: local deleted, free=$(free)GiB"
  else
    say "$lbl: VERIFY MISMATCH local=$tsz remote=$rsz -- keeping local copy"
    rm -f "/tmp/${lbl}.tgz"
  fi
}

move "$HOME/graphmark-bench"                        graphmark-bench
move "$HOME/devenv/graphify-parity-inputs"          graphify-parity-inputs
move "$HOME/distill-eval-work"                      distill-eval-work
move "$HOME/devenv/graphify-parity-artifacts"       graphify-parity-artifacts
say "DONE free=$(free)GiB"
EOF
chmod +x /tmp/mac_move_bench.sh
nohup bash /tmp/mac_move_bench.sh >/dev/null 2>&1 &
echo "launched, pid $!"
echo "target: gs://graphmark-evidence-504800/mac-offload-20260812/"
echo "log: ~/mac_move_bench.log"

content.text:
Here's the answer, and one piece of arithmetic in it cuts against the obvious choice.

## Recommendation: SWE-bench Pro (public set), with SWE-EVO as the mechanism cell

**[SWE-bench Pro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.16941)** hits every condition I measured:

| my win condition | SWE-bench Pro |
|---|---|
| long baseline sessions (74% win rate at 69–136 calls) | tasks take a professional engineer **hours to days** |
| cross-file changes (where `callers`/`impact` pay) | patches span **multiple files**, substantial modifications |
| uncontaminated repos (so localization is genuinely hard) | GPL + **18 proprietary commercial** repos, contamination-resistant by construction |
| correctness headroom | **<45% public, <20% commercial** — versus our suite's saturated 100% |
| enough n for power | **1,865 problems / 41 repos** |

That last row matters: our REP30F cell had baseline resolving 30/30, so no tool could show a correctness gain. Here the baseline fails most of the time, which is where a locator earns its keep.

**[SWE-EVO](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.18470v5)** is the purer test of the mechanism but too small to headline: **48 tasks, average 20.9 files edited per gold patch**, 874 tests, 2,390-word specs, and only 25% resolution for GPT-5.4/OpenHands versus 72.8% on SWE-bench Verified. A 21-file patch is exactly what `RELATED SITES` and `impact` exist for — I measured that label at only 10.1% precision on single-hunk SWE-bench patches, and on a 21-file change the base rate of genuinely-related files is far higher. But at n=48 my MDE is around 25 points, so it can demonstrate the mechanism, not carry the number.

I'm ruling out **[NL2Repo-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12730)** despite it being the most fashionable long-horizon option: it starts from an **empty workspace**, so there is no existing code to locate and the graph has literally nothing to index.

## The arithmetic, including the part that hurts

For 25% cost savings on `cost ≈ turns^1.179`, eg must use **21.7% fewer turns**. In my winning bin I measured eg 73.0 vs baseline 85.0 — only 14.1% fewer, giving +17.9%. To close that at B=85 the substitution ratio must reach **~7.95**; I measured **5.53**.

And here's the uncomfortable bit: **graph calls stayed flat at ~2.65–2.71 per session regardless of difficulty** (winners vs losers, p=0.91). If that holds on longer tasks, then as sessions grow the *absolute* displacement needed grows while the graph's call budget doesn't — so the percentage saving would **shrink**, not grow. Longer tasks only help if the ratio keeps climbing, i.e. each call prevents more flailing. It rose from −0.09 to +5.53 across my observed range, so reaching ~8 is a modest extrapolation — but it is an extrapolation, and extrapolating past the measured range is exactly what produced five withdrawn headlines here.

## Two traps to pre-register against before spending

**Selection on the gate.** With baselines failing >55%, the both-arms-succeed gate will drop most pairs, and survivors are non-random. Worse, failed baselines hit `max_turns`, which inflates baseline turns and manufactures eg savings. I'd pre-register the resolved-rate denominator as *attempted*, not *submitted* — the same error that nearly had me report 100% instead of 96.7% today.

**Repo-scale cost.** These are large proprietary codebases; the graph index build was already 3.7–9.1s on entire-graph, and that's the wall-clock tax that made eg 7.9% slower. PR #92 helps; it may not be enough.

The honest framing: this is the first benchmark I've seen where the win condition and the task shape actually line up, and I'd put the prediction at **+15% to +25%** with the mechanism endpoint (substitution ratio ≥ 7.9) as the thing that decides it — not the token total.

**Sources:** [SWE-bench Pro](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.16941) · [Scale leaderboard](https://labs.scale.com/leaderboard/swe_bench_pro_private) · [SWE-EVO](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.18470v5) · [NL2Repo-Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.12730) · [RoadmapBench](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.15846v1) · [Awesome-Repo-Level-Code-Generation](https://github.com/YerbaPage/Awesome-Repo-Level-Code-Generation)

content.text:
Yes — and the search surfaced the single most useful sentence in this whole line of work:

> "performance significantly deteriorates when handling **cross-file** issues"

That's the graph's exact job. Models are documented as weakest precisely where `impact`, `callers` and `RELATED SITES` operate.

## Recommendation: SWE-PolyBench verified, filtered to cross-file

**[SWE-PolyBench](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.08703)** (Amazon) — 2,110 full / **382 verified**. Its four languages are Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, and **every one sits in entire-graph's rich tier**:

```
TypeScript  18 relations      Java  16      Python  13      JavaScript  10
```

No dead weight. Compare that to what you're running now, where the suite is loaded with the graph's weakest languages: redis and valkey in **C (4 relations)**, three Ruby repos at **5**. You've been measuring the tool on the languages where it has almost no call graph to offer.

It also ships **per-language and per-complexity metrics plus a cross-file breakdown**, so the filter is available in the dataset rather than something I'd have to reconstruct.

**[Multi-SWE-bench](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.02605)** (ByteDance) is the runner-up: 8 languages, 2,132 instances, and the best resolved rate is only **19.32%** — far more headroom than SWE-PolyBench. But 2 of its 8 languages are C and C++ at 4 relations each. I'd run it with those subsets dropped, keeping Java/TS/JS/Go/Rust/Python, all rich tier.

## Why filtering to cross-file is legitimate here

This matters, because it's the opposite of the mistake I made earlier today. Selecting on **baseline turns** manufactured a fake +33% — that's conditioning on one arm's outcome. Selecting on **cross-file vs single-file** is a property of the task and the gold patch, fixed before either arm runs. It's arm-independent, so it's a fair stratification rather than a denominator trick. Pre-register it as a stratum, not a post-hoc cut.

## The arithmetic

For 25% I need the substitution ratio at ~7.9 (measured best: 5.53). Three things stack in the right direction on this target:

- **cross-file tasks** mean the 21-files-per-patch shape where `RELATED SITES` precision should rise well above the 10.1% I measured on single-hunk SWE-bench patches
- **rich-tier languages only** mean `impact` returns real blast radius instead of `CONTAINS/DEFINES`
- **19–43% resolution** means real flailing, versus the saturated 100% baseline that made our suite unable to show anything

Honest prediction: **+15% to +25%**, and I'd hold the mechanism endpoint as primary — ratio ≥ 7.9 and cross-file localization improving — because a token total at n≈380 still can't separate a working tool from a baseline that flailed.

The cheap first move is free: **replay the language-relation profile against your existing results.** I can check right now whether your measured per-language savings correlate with relation count (18/16/13/10 vs 4/5). If TypeScript and Java are already outperforming C and Ruby in the data you have, that validates the whole thesis for $0 before you buy a single new cell.

**Sources:** [SWE-PolyBench paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.08703) · [SWE-PolyBench repo](https://github.com/amazon-science/SWE-PolyBench) · [AWS announcement](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/amazon-introduces-swe-polybench-a-multi-lingual-benchmark-for-ai-coding-agents/) · [Multi-SWE-bench](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.02605) · [Multi-SWE-bench leaderboard](https://llm-stats.com/benchmarks/multi-swe-bench) · [SWE-bench Multilingual](https://www.swebench.com/multilingual.html)

content.text:
Two findings, one blocking:

**`datacurve/deep-swe` is GATED** — requires HuggingFace authentication. I can't build a DeepSWE v1.1 harness without an HF token that has access. That one needs you.

**SWE-PolyBench_500 turns out to be even better than I expected**: exactly 125 each of Java/JavaScript/TypeScript/Python (all rich-tier), plus per-instance `Dockerfile` and task-intrinsic complexity labels (`is_single_func`, `is_mixed`, `modified_nodes`, `num_class_changes`) — which is exactly the arm-independent stratification I said we'd need.

Building the SWE-bench Pro harness now:

input.command:
SP=/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-suhaan-devenv/b0108f24-43a4-413e-94c9-bd361b6fafc5/scratchpad
cat > "$SP/build_pro_tasks.py" <<'PY'
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""SWE-bench Pro -> graphmark task schema, plus a coverage-stratified 5-instance pilot.

Pro field names differ from the suite's (lowercase f2p/p2p) and its test IDs are
"file | testname" strings rather than pytest node ids, so the mapping is explicit
rather than a rename.
"""
import json, os, re, collections, random
from datasets import load_dataset

S = os.path.expanduser("~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench")
d = load_dataset("ScaleAI/SWE-bench_Pro", split="test")

def jl(x):
    if isinstance(x, list): return x
    if not x: return []
    try: return json.loads(x)
    except Exception: return [x]

LANG = {"go":"Go","python":"Python","js":"JavaScript","ts":"TypeScript"}
inst = []
for r in d:
    files = sorted(set(re.findall(r'^\+\+\+ b/(\S+)', r["patch"] or "", re.M)))
    inst.append({
        "instance_id":      r["instance_id"],
        "repo":             r["repo"],
        "base_commit":      r["base_commit"],
        "problem_statement":r["problem_statement"],
        "FAIL_TO_PASS":     jl(r["fail_to_pass"]),
        "PASS_TO_PASS":     jl(r["pass_to_pass"]),
        "language":         LANG.get(r["repo_language"], r["repo_language"]),
        "hints_text":       "",
        "created_at":       "",
        # Pro-specific, carried through for the runner/grader
        "pro_interface":        r["interface"],
        "pro_requirements":     r["requirements"],
        "pro_test_files":       jl(r["selected_test_files_to_run"]),
        "pro_before_repo_cmd":  r["before_repo_set_cmd"],
        "pro_test_patch":       r["test_patch"],
        "gold_files":           files,
        "gold_file_count":      len(files),
    })
json.dump({"instances": inst}, open(f"{S}/tasks/swebench_pro_731.json","w"))
print(f"  wrote tasks/swebench_pro_731.json  ({len(inst)} instances)")

by = collections.Counter(i["language"] for i in inst)
print(f"  languages: {dict(by)}")
mf = sum(1 for i in inst if i["gold_file_count"] > 1)
print(f"  multi-file: {mf}/{len(inst)} = {mf/len(inst):.1%}   mean files {sum(i['gold_file_count'] for i in inst)/len(inst):.1f}")

# ---- coverage-stratified pilot: every language represented, multi-file only,
#      median-ish size so the pilot is not a freak instance. NOT proportional --
#      labelled so nobody later reads a 5-pair pilot as an effect estimate.
rnd = random.Random(20260812)
pilot = []
for lang, k in (("Go",2), ("Python",1), ("JavaScript",1), ("TypeScript",1)):
    pool = [i for i in inst if i["language"] == lang and 2 <= i["gold_file_count"] <= 8]
    pool.sort(key=lambda i: i["instance_id"])
    pilot += rnd.sample(pool, min(k, len(pool)))
json.dump({"instances": pilot}, open(f"{S}/tasks/pro_pilot5.json","w"))
print(f"\n  wrote tasks/pro_pilot5.json ({len(pilot)} instances, coverage-stratified)")
for i in pilot:
    print(f"    {i['language']:11} {i['instance_id'][:58]:58} files={i['gold_file_count']} repo={i['repo']}")
PY

**PRO5 is running.** All 11 preflight gates passed, 5 shards up, 0 fatals, 0 fairness aborts.

```
1  machine idle              0 sessions
2  results for tag           0
3  prereg                    1d5ffcb133427cec
4  graphs ready              5/5
5  FAIRNESS_STRICT           1
6  VERIFY in eg-q            0
7  eg-q size                 1268 (clean fold-free)
8  repo caches               4/4
9  decoded prompts           0 wrapped in quotes
10 auth probe                OK
11 disk                      857G free
```

Two things the gates earned today: **gate 9** exists only because I checked the encoding and found 985 double-encoded fields — without it the agents would have received one giant line of literal `\n`. And **gate 10** is the live-auth probe I rewrote after the old env-var check went green on a box where `claude` reported "Not logged in"; it correctly refused the first launch attempt because I'd deleted the credential.

The fairness story here is the cleanest of any cell today: **zero diff from the audited config.** `run_rep30f.sh` is used verbatim and only `TASKS_FILE` differs, so `PUBLISHED_EXACT`, `FAIRNESS_STRICT`, `EG_VERIFY_MODE=off`, prompt-symmetry asserts and netjail-both-arms are inherited by construction rather than re-declared by me.

What I'll report when it drains, per the sealed prereg — and what I won't:

**Will report:** whether the harness works end-to-end (prompt delivery 10/10, eg tool block non-empty on all 5 eg sessions and 0 B on all 5 baseline, graph actually invoked, patches collected clean under the PR #70 filters), plus the mechanism — graph calls per session, substitution ratio, and index latency on those monorepos where builds took 163s and 109s versus 9–24s on flipt.

**Won't report as a result:** any savings number. Five pairs against a ~25-point MDE is noise, and two identical cells here have differed 8.57% with no intervention at all. That's written into the prereg so it can't be quietly reinterpreted later.

Also expected and pre-registered: some sessions may hit `CC_MAX_TURNS=120`, since Pro tasks are hours-to-days of human work. If they do I'll say so rather than gate them out silently. And no correctness grading — Pro's `fail_to_pass` are `"file | testname"` strings that the swebench grader can't parse, so that needs its own adapter.

content.text:
**Verified. The harness is real, complete, and the fairness design is sound** — arguably tighter than the SWE-bench one.

**Data provenance: clean.** Apache-2.0 on the harness, per-task upstream licenses all permissive (MIT / Apache-2.0 / BSD-3-Clause), explicitly documented as "none are copyleft or share-alike". 117 tasks with full provenance table.

**Task spec: proper containerized format.** `task.toml` at `schema_version 1.3` with `language`, `repository_url`, `base_commit_hash`, a `[verifier]` block, plus `environment/`, `tests/`, `solution/`, `pre_artifacts.sh`, and `instruction.md`. Real evaluation infrastructure, not a task list.

**Multi-language, which is what you asked for:** Go, Python, TypeScript across `abs-lang/abs`, `PyCQA/bandit`, `arktypeio/arktype`, `mattn/anko`, `rhysd/actionlint`, `reagento/adaptix`, `aio-libs/aiomonitor`, `jeffijoe/awilix`.

**Fairness — this is the part I'd defend.** From `arm_agent.py`'s own header: all arms are subclasses of Pier's stock ClaudeCode agent "so the agent scaffold, model plumbing and trajectory capture are **byte-identical** across arms", with the *only* difference being the tool block appended to the instruction — and it says byte-identical "by construction, not by convention", mirroring the `_assert_prompt_symmetry` check in the SWE-bench harness. That's the same discipline I've been enforcing, already built in.

**Four arms**, not two: `baseline / eg / eg-loc / graphify`. Baseline gets no tool and no TOOL block. There's also an explicit guard against partial cells — "have N complete task-quartets, not 48 baselines and nothing else."

**Prior runs already happened:** `dsw12x4_progress.tsv` shows a 12-task × 4-arm batch with `rc=0`, and graph build times from 7s to 773s.

**114 of 117 graphs prebuilt** — 3 missing, which I'd need to identify before a run.

So my earlier claim was wrong on two counts and I should be plain about it: DeepSWE is **not** blocked on gated HuggingFace access (the dataset ships inside the harness), and we **had** already built a harness. I told you otherwise because I searched HuggingFace instead of looking in the directory I had just archived — and I archived that 2.0G directory to GCS an hour ago without inspecting its contents, which is exactly the check I'd have insisted on from anyone else.

Steps to run it, now that it's restored to `~/restore/graphmark-bench/deepswe`:

1. **Relocate** it under the suite (`~/pe1/graphmark/deepswe`) so its relative paths resolve
2. **Identify the 3 missing graphs** and build them with `harness/build_graphs.sh`
3. **Verify the toolbox** — `make_toolbox.sh` copies `graphify-q.impl` and `_gqy.py` into `/opt/armtool` in-container; confirm the eg arm's binary is the current one, not a stale build
4. **Confirm arm symmetry live** by diffing the emitted instruction across arms on one task, since I've been burned by asserted-but-undelivered blocks
5. **Freeze a sample** with `freeze_sample.py`, then `run_sample.sh`
6. **Score** with `score.py`

One caveat before spending: PRO5 is running right now and load contention is an arm confound I have measured flipping signs. I'd let PRO5 drain first. Want me to do steps 1–4 (all free, no sessions) while it finishes?

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Scores PRO5 against sealed prereg 1d5ffcb133427cec.

n=5 caveat attached, per the prereg."""
import json, os, glob, re, collections, statistics as st

S = os.path.expanduser("~/pe1/graphmark/agentic-swebench")
TAG = "PRO5"
GRAPH = re.compile(r"(?:^|[|;&`(]|&&|\|\|)\s*(?:\S*/)?(?:eg|eg-q)\s+|(?:^|[|;&`(]|&&|\|\|)\s*entire\s+graph\b")
CONTAM = re.compile(r"^\+\+\+ b/.*(?:[Rr][Ee][Pp][Rr][Oo]|/out/|^out/|\.class$|explore|scratch)", re.M)

def usage(J):
    u = J.get("usage") or {}
    g = lambda *k: next((u[x] for x in k if u.get(x) is not None), 0)
    return (g("input_tokens") + g("output_tokens")
            + g("cache_read_input_tokens","cache_read_tokens")
            + g("cache_creation_input_tokens","cache_creation_tokens"))

rec, drops = {}, collections.Counter()
for arm in ("eg","baseline"):
    for d in sorted(glob.glob(f"{S}/results/{TAG}_r1_{arm}/{arm}/*/")):
        iid = os.path.basename(d.rstrip("/"))
        f, p, tb = d+"cc_out.json", d+"patch.diff", d+"tool_block.txt"
        e = {"dir": d,
             "has_prompt":  os.path.exists(d+"prompt.txt") and os.path.getsize(d+"prompt.txt")>0,
             "tb_bytes":    os.path.getsize(tb) if os.path.exists(tb) else -1,
             "patch_bytes": os.path.getsize(p) if os.path.exists(p) else 0,
             "gq_lines":    sum(1 for _ in open(d+"gq_calls.log",errors="ignore")) if os.path.exists(d+"gq_calls.log") else 0,
             "invariant":   open(d+"prompt_invariant.sha256").read().strip() if os.path.exists(d+"prompt_invariant.sha256") else ""}
        if os.path.exists(p) and os.path.getsize(p)>0:
            e["contam"] = bool(CONTAM.search(open(p,errors="ignore").read()))
        else:
            e["contam"] = False
        if os.path.exists(f):
            raw = open(f,errors="ignore").read()
            e["corrupt"] = "CORRUPT_CC_OUT" in raw
            try:
                J = json.loads(raw); J = J[0] if isinstance(J,list) else J
                e.update(subtype=J.get("subtype"), is_error=bool(J.get("is_error")),
                         turns=J.get("num_turns") or 0, cost=J.get("total_cost_usd") or 0,
                         tok=usage(J), ms=J.get("duration_ms") or 0)
            except Exception:
                e["subtype"] = "unparseable"
        else:
            e["subtype"] = "missing"
        rec[(arm,iid)] = e

# transcript: real graph calls + total tool calls
calls = collections.defaultdict(lambda: {"tot":0,"graph":0})
for arm in ("eg","baseline"):
    for f in glob.glob(f"{S}/results/{TAG}_r1_{arm}/ccfg/projects/*/*.jsonl"):
        iid=None; tot=g=0
        for ln in open(f,errors="ignore"):
            ln=ln.strip()
            if not ln or ln[0]!="{": continue
            try: r=json.loads(ln)
            except Exception: continue
            if iid is None and r.get("cwd"): iid=os.path.basename(r["cwd"])
            if r.get("type")!="assistant": continue
            c=(r.get("message") or {}).get("content")
            if not isinstance(c,list): continue
            for b in c:
                if isinstance(b,dict) and b.get("type")=="tool_use":
                    tot+=1
                    if b.get("name") in ("Bash","bash") and GRAPH.search((b.get("input") or {}).get("command") or ""): g+=1
        if iid: calls[(arm,iid)]["tot"]+=tot; calls[(arm,iid)]["graph"]+=g

egs  = [v for (a,i),v in rec.items() if a=="eg"]
base = [v for (a,i),v in rec.items() if a=="baseline"]
print(f"=== {TAG} — prereg 1d5ffcb133427cec (HARNESS SMOKE TEST, not an effect estimate) ===")
print(f"  sessions on disk: eg {len(egs)}  baseline {len(base)}")

print("\n=== PRIMARY 1: DELIVERY ===")
print(f"  prompt emitted:              {sum(1 for e in egs+base if e['has_prompt'])}/{len(egs)+len(base)}  (need 10/10)")
print(f"  eg tool_block non-empty:     {sum(1 for e in egs if e['tb_bytes']>0)}/{len(egs)}  (need all)")
print(f"  baseline tool_block 0 B:     {sum(1 for e in base if e['tb_bytes']==0)}/{len(base)}  (need all)")
egb = sorted({e['tb_bytes'] for e in egs if e['tb_bytes']>0})
print(f"  eg tool_block sizes:         {egb}")
print("\n=== PRIMARY 2: GRAPH REACHABLE ===")
print(f"  eg sessions with >=1 logged graph call: {sum(1 for e in egs if e['gq_lines']>0)}/{len(egs)}")
gcalls=[calls[('eg',os.path.basename(e['dir'].rstrip('/')))]['graph'] for e in egs]
print(f"  transcript graph calls/session: {gcalls}  mean {st.mean(gcalls) if gcalls else 0:.2f}")
print(f"  baseline graph calls (must be 0): {sum(calls[('baseline',os.path.basename(e['dir'].rstrip('/')))]['graph'] for e in base)}")
print("\n=== PRIMARY 3: PATCH COLLECTION ===")
for lab,g in (("eg",egs),("baseline",base)):
    ne=sum(1 for e in g if e['patch_bytes']>0)
    print(f"  {lab:9} non-empty patches {ne}/{len(g)}   contaminated {sum(1 for e in g if e['contam'])}   "

print("\n=== PRIMARY 4: SESSION OUTCOMES ===")
for lab,g in (("eg",egs),("baseline",base)):
    print(f"  {lab:9} " + "  ".join(f"{k}={v}" for k,v in collections.Counter(e.get('subtype') for e in g).items())

          + f"   hit_turn_cap(>=120)={sum(1 for e in g if (e.get('turns') or 0)>=120)}")

    if not b: continue

    if ok(v) and ok(b): pairs.append((i,v,b))
print(f"\n=== GATE: {len(pairs)}/5 pairs ===")
if pairs:
    print("\n=== SECONDARY (mechanism) ===")
    ce=st.mean([calls[('eg',i)]['tot'] for i,_,_ in pairs]); cb=st.mean([calls[('baseline',i)]['tot'] for i,_,_ in pairs])
    gg=st.mean([calls[('eg',i)]['graph'] for i,_,_ in pairs])
    print(f"  eg calls/session {ce:.2f}   baseline {cb:.2f}   graph {gg:.2f}")
    if gg: print(f"  substitution ratio {((cb-ce)+gg)/gg:.3f}   (Opus SWE-bench ref 0.980)")
    print(f"  turns: eg {st.mean([v.get('turns',0) for _,v,_ in pairs]):.1f}  baseline {st.mean([b.get('turns',0) for _,_,b in pairs]):.1f}")
    print(f"  wall-clock: eg {st.mean([v.get('ms',0) for _,v,_ in pairs])/60000:.1f}min  baseline {st.mean([b.get('ms',0) for _,_,b in pairs])/60000:.1f}min")
    te=sum(v['tok'] for _,v,_ in pairs); tb2=sum(b['tok'] for _,_,b in pairs)

    print(f"  !! n={len(pairs)} — MDE at n=30 is ~25pt and identical cells differ 8.57%.")
    print(f"  !! These are NOT an effect estimate. Prereg forbids quoting them as savings.")

That's a mechanism I haven't refuted. But it's now the *only* live hypothesis, and it's worth about the difference between a 10.1%-precision `RELATED SITES` label and a useful one — not obviously 25%.

So bin 5's +17.9% is substantially a selection artifact, not a harvestable effect.

content.text:
Your logic is directionally right, and the data agrees with the *sign* — but not the magnitude. Here's the properly-specified test, 21 cells, unit of analysis = cell so there's no selection artifact:

```
r(population mean turns, cell savings) = +0.363    p = 0.1096   NOT significant
short cells (<57 turns):  +1.47%   n=10
long  cells (>=57 turns): +4.50%   n=11
```

So longer populations do average better. **But look at what actually happens at 60+ turns:**

```
SMOKE12    60.4 turns   +25.27%   n=12
ER12       62.0          +2.01%   n=11
PE1SAMP    63.3          -3.89%   n=9
HAIKU50    63.6          -5.84%   n=47
HOLD50     63.6          +2.16%   n=48
SHIP12     65.4          +2.00%   n=10
RUNG2      65.8          +1.58%   n=10
                 mean:   +3.33%
```

A 60+ turn benchmark buys about **+3 points, not 25.** And notice the spread at essentially identical length: HAIKU50 at 63.6 turns gives −5.84% while HOLD50 at 63.6 turns gives +2.16%. **The between-cell variance at fixed session length is larger than the entire length effect.**

There's also a tell in that table you should see: every extreme positive is small-n. SMOKER12W +33.47% (n=12), SMOKE12 +25.27% (n=12). The four cells with n≥45 land at +2.90%, +2.16%, −5.84%, +12.86%. That's the signature of noise, not of a length effect — big samples regress to ~2-3%, small ones scatter.

So to answer you directly: **you're right that turns matter, and wrong that it's enough.** Turn count is the only predictor that survives at all, it's real in direction, it's not statistically significant at n=21 cells, and it's worth single digits. Finding a 60-turn benchmark doesn't get you to 25% because the effect isn't that big and the noise at any fixed length swamps it.

And the reason bin 5 looked like +17.9% is the denominator problem: savings is (base − eg)/base, so selecting instances where base ran long selects cases where base was high partly by luck. That's why splitting on baseline turns manufactured +33% while an arm-independent split gave p=0.33. The bin-5 number was never harvestable.

The one hypothesis I still haven't refuted is the multi-file one — 85.6% of Pro's patches touch multiple files and `impact`/`RELATED SITES` have never been tested where they should matter. PRO5 answers that directly, it's already paid for, and it's the last live idea I have.

content.text:
Straight answer, no hedging.

## What defines a winner or loser

```
savings = (baseline_cost - eg_cost) / baseline_cost
```

A winner is a run where the **baseline happened to waste calls**. A loser is a run where it didn't. That's it.

Three measurements make that concrete:

- **eg behaves identically either way.** Graph calls in winners vs losers: 2.68 vs 2.65, permutation **p=0.9128**. Nothing eg does distinguishes a win from a loss.
- **The graph is a 1:1 substitute.** It displaces 0.980 calls per call it makes. It swaps grep calls for graph calls; it doesn't remove work.
- **Winner-ness is not a property of the task.** Same instance, run twice: savings correlate **r=+0.014**. It wins one time and loses the next. Win rate across 489 pairs: **49.9%**. A coin flip.

## So which benchmark has the winners we want

**None. That's the answer, and I should have reached it before proposing three of them.**

Winner-ness isn't a task property, so it can't be selected by choosing a dataset. Everything measurable in advance is dead:

```
repo size (log symbols)        r = -0.039   p = 0.72    n = 599
issue length                   r = -0.036
stack trace present            r = +0.014
file paths named in issue      r = -0.028
repo identity                              p = 0.1676
learned difficulty predictor  rho = 0.193  (needed 0.60)
cell-level session length      r = +0.363   p = 0.11    worth +3pt
```

The only thing that correlates at all is baseline session length, and that's the *outcome of the run in the arm we're comparing against*. You cannot pick it in advance, and selecting on it afterwards manufactures fake savings — it gave +33% where an arm-independent split gave p=0.33, because baseline sits in the denominator.

## The thing underneath all of it

Here's the number that explains why no benchmark can save this: **eg reaches a gold file in 4.77 tool calls; the no-tool baseline reaches it in 3.62.** It wins that race 13 times out of 91.

The graph is currently *slower at its own job* than grep. That is not a property of SWE-bench, or of language mix, or of repo size — it's the tool. No benchmark makes a slower locator faster. Fix retrieval so the first graph call lands on the gold file and beats grep, and then every benchmark works, this one included.

So the honest ranking of where effort belongs: **tool retrieval quality first, benchmark choice a distant last.** I spent today's search on the wrong end of that, and your pushback is what surfaced it.

PRO5 still finishes and still answers the one open question — whether `impact`/`RELATED SITES` earn their keep on 85.6%-multi-file patches, which has never been tested. That's a *tool capability* question, which is the right kind. But I'm not going to tell you another dataset will fix this.

```

  eg        n=36   mean 5.64   median 5.0
  baseline  n=33   mean 3.85   median 4.0

```

**So no — we can't make it faster than grep by improving retrieval, because retrieval isn't what's broken.** In more than half of sessions the graph hands the agent a gold file on its very first call, and the agent *still* takes 5.64 calls to open one — slower than an agent with no tool at all, which gets there in 3.85.

The graph is not failing to find the code. It finds it, says so immediately, and the agent goes and looks around anyway. That single fact explains everything else measured today: the 0.980 substitution ratio, the ~0% savings, the 49.9% win rate, and why eleven payload levers all landed on nothing. You can't save calls by answering faster when the answer was never the constraint.

**Can Pro do 25%?** No. Its sessions run 34–72 turns (mean 49.2), which is no longer than our existing cells, and the cell-level length effect is worth about +3 points and isn't significant (p=0.11). The only thing Pro still tests that nothing else has is whether `impact`/`RELATED SITES` earn their keep on 85.6%-multi-file patches — and that's a tool-capability question, not a benchmark question.

**And this reframes what "make it faster than grep" would require.** Not better ranking — gold is already in the first payload over half the time and ranked 1–3. It requires the agent to *act* on a correct answer instead of verifying it. Every attempt at that has failed or backfired: the shipped doctrine block drove graph calls from 2.00 to 1.12 and cost 24 points; the edit-ready payload displaced 0.42 of 3.71 reads; source-folding into grep output measured −9.50%.

That's a genuinely hard wall, and it isn't in the benchmark. If you want 25%, the target is: **get calls-to-gold from 5.64 below baseline's 3.85** — a concrete, cheap-to-measure number that any change can be tested against offline before spending a cent. That's the first metric I've found today that is both causal and directly attackable.

I'd let PRO5 finish since it answers the multi-file question, and I'd stop looking for benchmarks. Want me to dig into *why* the agent doesn't act on the first payload — the 16 of 36 sessions where it had the answer and went exploring anyway? That's where the 25% would have to come from, and it costs nothing to look.

content.text:
Yes — and this **corrects what I told you a message ago.** I said the agent ignores a correct answer. It doesn't:

```
n=21 sessions where the first payload named a gold file

very next action:        read 52.4% · graph 19.0% · ls/find 14.3% · grep 9.5% · cat/sed 4.8%
first file it opened:    GOLD 76.2%  ·  not-gold 23.8%
actions between having the answer and touching gold:  mean 2.60, MEDIAN 0.0
touched gold immediately (0 intervening actions):     11/20 = 55%
```

When the payload is right, the agent behaves well: it reads next half the time, the first file it opens is the gold file **76%** of the time, and the median number of intervening actions is **zero**. The mean of 2.60 is a tail, not the typical case. My "goes and looks around anyway" was wrong — I read a mean and ignored the median, which is the same mistake that produced the −151% equal-weighted figure earlier today.

So where does 5.64 come from? Not from acting. From the **44.4% of sessions where the first payload did not name a gold file** (16 of 36). Those sessions have to keep searching, and they drag the mean.

**That makes it a retrieval problem after all, and a specific one:** first-payload gold-hit rate is **55.6%**. Raise that and the slow tail shrinks directly, because the acting behaviour downstream is already good. That's the opposite conclusion from the one I gave you, and it's the more hopeful one.

Concretely fixable, in rough order of promise:
- **First-call hit rate 55.6% → higher.** Every previous lever aimed at payload *shape* (edit-ready regions, source folding, doctrine text). None aimed at *whether the right file is in there at all*. That's untried.
- **The 23.8% where it opens a non-gold file first** — the payload named gold but something else outranked it, so ranking within the payload matters even though gold is "in the top 3".
- The target is now a single number I can measure offline against stored payloads for zero dollars: **calls-to-gold 5.64, needs to beat baseline's 3.85.**

Two honest caveats. **n=21 is small** — this needs the same treatment at n≥100 before I'd build on it, and I've been burned by exactly this size of sample today. And a higher hit rate has to come from real ranking improvements, not from widening the payload, because widening costs prefix bytes that eat the gain.

But to answer you plainly: **yes, it looks fixable, and this is the first lever today that attacks a cause rather than a symptom.** I'd verify the 55.6% at scale first — free, and it decides whether the whole thing is worth building.

content.text:
This refutes what I told you one message ago, and I should say so directly.

```
CALLS-TO-GOLD, split by whether the first payload named a gold file
  eg  HIT   n=20   mean 5.40   median 3.0
  eg  MISS  n=16   mean 5.94   median 5.0
  baseline  n=34   mean 4.79   median 4.5

WHAT RAISING THE HIT RATE IS WORTH
  hit rate    calls-to-gold   calls saved   cost gain   total
    55.6%          5.64           0.00        0.00%     2.50%
    80.0%          5.51           0.13        0.16%     2.66%
   100.0%          5.40           0.24        0.29%     2.79%
```

**Hitting barely helps.** A MISS costs only 0.54 calls more than a HIT. So driving the hit rate from 55.6% to a perfect 100% is worth **+0.29 percentage points**. My "this is the first lever that attacks a cause" was wrong — I assumed the miss sessions were expensive without checking, which is the third time today I've built on an unmeasured premise.

There's also a sign instability you should know about: by **median**, a hit session reaches gold in 3.0 calls versus baseline's 4.5 — eg wins. By **mean** it's 5.40 versus 4.79 — eg loses. A tail of slow hit-sessions flips the direction. At n=20/16/34 neither reading is trustworthy.

**And here is the arithmetic that closes the whole localization thesis.** Calls-to-gold is ~5 out of a ~50-call session — **10% of the work.** Even if the graph teleported the agent to the gold file in zero calls, the ceiling is about 10% of calls ≈ 12% cost. We are fighting over half a call inside a slice that can't reach 25% even when perfected.

**So: can a benchmark do it in current state? No.** The fair number is +2.5% (n=75) to +3.5% (n=489), the best population-level effect is +4.5% for long-session cells at p=0.11, and every task-intrinsic selector is dead — repo size r=−0.039 at n=599, issue features under |0.08|, learned predictor rho=0.193. Choosing a dataset cannot manufacture an effect that isn't in the tool.

**And if we fix retrieval? +2.79%.** Not 25%.

The honest summary of where 25% would have to come from: not localization, not benchmark choice, not payload shape, not gating, not a cheaper model. It would have to come from the graph eliminating work in the other **90%** of the session — the build/test/verify/edit loop — which is not what a code-search tool does. That's the finding, and I think it's the real one.

content.text:
Here's the honest answer, built on the whole day's measurements.

## The structural problem

```
a session is ~50 tool calls
  grep          14.59        cat/sed   12.55        find/ls    6.39
  Read           4.19        Edit       3.98        other sh   3.45
  Write          2.88        GRAPH      2.71
localization (calls-to-gold) ~5 calls  =  10% of the session
```

**entire-graph operates on 10% of the work and touches 2.71 of 50 calls.** Even perfected — instant, always-correct localization — the ceiling is ~12% cost. 25% is not reachable inside the tool's current job description. That isn't a benchmark problem or a tuning problem; it's a scope problem.

## What would have to be fixed, in order of arithmetic weight

**1. The substitution ratio must exceed 1.0.** It's 0.980 — the graph swaps one call for one call. Every call it makes must remove *more than one*, which means answering questions that currently cost multiple calls. The measured multi-call pattern is grep refinement chains: 5.51/session, of which **62% are wrong-guess** — the agent tried a different string entirely. That's the biggest addressable pool and it needs retrieval that works when the literal token is wrong. I measured that the graph already knew the eventual target in 28.9% of those cases, so the information exists; what failed was delivering it (a safe grep interception only fires on literal misses, and those overlap the mechanism just 8.6% of the time).

**2. It has to matter after the edit.** 97.7% of the cost difference is post-edit, and 86% of graph use is pre-edit. The graph helps you find code, then goes quiet exactly when the session gets expensive — verification, test runs, regression chasing. This was tried: the post-edit rider *added* 4.2 turns per session.

**3. It has to get used instead of grep.** 14.59 shell greps versus 2.71 graph calls. Instructions backfire — shipping the vendor doctrine drove graph calls from 2.00 to 1.12 and cost 24 points.

All three have been attempted and all three failed. I'd want you to hear that plainly rather than get a fourth variation of the same lever.

## What I'd actually fix

**The claim, not the code.** The tool's measured effect is +2.5% tokens with a **7.9% wall-clock penalty** and no correctness benefit on a suite where the baseline already resolves 30/30. "Saves tokens" isn't supportable at a size anyone would notice. What *is* supportable and useful: it's a deterministic, local, no-egress code locator whose first answer names a gold file 55.6% of the time and, when it does, gets there in a median 3 calls versus grep's 4.5. That's a real capability claim with a real number behind it.

**Then the two things already shipped today,** which are genuine and unglamorous: PR #92 cuts index latency 28x on warm repeats and directly attacks the wall-clock penalty, which is the cost a user actually feels. PR #70 stops `Repro.java` and compiled `.class` files being graded as the model's answer, which had already overturned a published quality claim.

**And if you want to keep chasing savings,** the honest next step is not another benchmark or another payload tweak — it's picking one of the three items above and pre-registering the mechanism endpoint before spending. The cheapest is #1: I can measure offline, for zero dollars, whether a semantic-fallback retrieval would answer the 62% wrong-guess pool. If it can't, the ratio can't exceed 1.0 and the whole savings thesis is finished.

I've been wrong three times today in the direction of optimism — the gate, the shim, and the hit-rate fix all looked promising until measured. So take this as the pattern rather than an accident: the levers keep failing because the tool is sized for 10% of the session, and no amount of tuning changes the denominator.

prefix check but escape via symlink.

both patches and find the entry points they did NOT cover. A prefix check like
strings.HasPrefix(path, repoRoot) is bypassable by /repo-evil when repoRoot=/repo; verify whether the
current code uses a proper boundary (repoRoot + separator) EVERYWHERE, and grep for any remaining
HasPrefix path check. Sinks: os.ReadFile, os.Open, filepath.Join with unvalidated input.
The prize finding: a repo whose content causes the tool to read and PRINT a file outside the repo

    prompt: `SURFACE 3: SYMLINKS, TOCTOU, AND WRITE PRIMITIVES.
The provider walks the working tree and writes caches. Check:
 - does the tree walk follow symlinks OUT of the repo and index/print their contents? (filepath.Walk

 - a repo containing a symlink to /etc/passwd or ~/.ssh: is it read, indexed, or emitted?

      agent(`${COMMON}

    finder missed? Look specifically for one.

${JSON.stringify(clean.map(c => ({ surface: c.surface, clean: c.report && c.report.surfaces_checked_clean, titles: (c.report && c.report.findings || []).map(f => f.title) })), null, 1)}

overflow/truncation in size or line arithmetic; TOCTOU between stat and read; unicode/normalization

        top_unexplored: { type: 'array', maxItems: 3, items: { type: 'string' } },
      },
    } })

const judge = agent(`${COMMON}

FINAL TRIAGE. Below are all findings with adversarial verdicts. Produce the maintainer-facing report.

${JSON.stringify(allVerdicts, null, 1)}

Rules:

 - Rank by realistic bug-bounty / CVE likelihood: how easily an outside reporter finds it, whether it
   crosses a real security boundary, and blast radius.
 - For each surviving finding give: title, severity, CWE, file:line, one-line exploit, minimal fix.
 - Call out any finding that is an INCOMPLETE PRIOR FIX (#88/#90/#91/#95/#96) -- those are the most
   likely to be reported, because the patch advertises the bug class.

   SECURITY.md / coordinated disclosure path.`,
  { label: 'final-triage', phase: 'Judge',
    schema: {
      type: 'object', additionalProperties: false,
      required: ['bottom_line', 'confirmed', 'most_likely_report', 'process_gaps'],
      properties: {
        bottom_line: { type: 'string', description: 'honest one-paragraph verdict on the codebase security posture' },
        confirmed: { type: 'array', maxItems: 14, items: { type: 'object', additionalProperties: false,
          required: ['title', 'severity', 'cwe', 'location', 'exploit', 'fix', 'incomplete_prior_fix'],
          properties: {
            title: { type: 'string' }, severity: { type: 'string' }, cwe: { type: 'string' },
            location: { type: 'string' }, exploit: { type: 'string' }, fix: { type: 'string' },
            incomplete_prior_fix: { type: 'string', description: 'which prior PR it re-opens, or "no"' },
          } } },
        most_likely_report: { type: 'string' },
        process_gaps: { type: 'array', maxItems: 6, items: { type: 'string' } },
      },
    } })

const [criticOut, judgeOut] = await Promise.all([critic, judge])
return { surfaces: clean, verdicts: allVerdicts, critic: criticOut, triage: judgeOut }

content.text:
The eight finders are still deep-reading 148K LOC. Two things are already verified and both matter now.

## I introduced a real bug, and it's merged on main

My PR #92 gate is unsound. The indexer admits a file on `Supported(path) || shebangRoutable(path)` (`provider_parallel.go:63`), but my gate forgives a dirty path on `extensionUnsupported(path)` alone (`search_cache.go:151`) — and `shebangRoutable` never looks at the extension. So a file with an unsupported extension *and* a shebang is indexed but invisible to cache invalidation. I reproduced it:

```
run1 (cold)                    cache_hit=False  symbols=2  files_indexed=1
run2 (warm, clean)             cache_hit=True   symbols=2  files_indexed=1
run3 untracked tool.txt with
     #!/usr/bin/env python     cache_hit=True   symbols=2  files_indexed=2   <-- STALE
run4 untracked .go (control)   cache_hit=False  symbols=4  files_indexed=3   <-- correct
```

Run 3 is the defect: `files_indexed=2` proves the indexer read `tool.txt`, yet a cached 2-symbol snapshot was served and its `gamma()` never appears. Silent stale results.

I predicted this exact class in my own PR text — "an extensionless path counts as supported, because a shebang can make it a script" — and then only guarded the extensionless case. A reviewer had already patched one hole in the same predicate before merge (`|| isManifestImportFile(path)`), which is the second instance of the same mistake. The fix is to make the gate call the indexer's own admission test rather than a parallel approximation.

**This is a correctness bug, not a CVE.** An attacker gains nothing they couldn't get by not writing the file. I'm reporting it under a security review because cache-integrity failures are where security bugs hide, and because it's my code and it's live.

## The shell injection was real, and is genuinely fixed

The `#90` vulnerability was not theoretical. A file named `test_gizmo;touch PWNED_BY_VERIFY;.py` under a `pytest.ini` caused the derived `VERIFY:` line to carry the payload, and since the shipped agent guide instructs agents to *run that exact command*, cloning a hostile repo and following the tool's own instructions executed attacker code. The finder reproduced `PWNED_BY_VERIFY` on the pre-fix path.

At `cceb4de` it's correctly closed. I checked the escaping myself: `shellQuote` uses the exact `shlex.quote` allowlist `_@%+=:,./-` with a correct `'` → `'\''` fallback, and `shellQuotePath` prefixes `./` so option-shaped filenames can't become flags. That's right.

## One non-security finding you should see anyway

The README now publishes an 8-system LoCoMo table with entire-graph first at **94.74 vs mem0 93.83**, and the docs sequence stripped every statistical caveat off that page — commit `4c21a82`, pushed directly with no PR, removed the significance sentence. `docs/benchmarks.md` still says the margin over the strongest inference-built competitor is **not significant**, and `LOCOMO-COMPARISON.md` self-discloses that the headline run id `sw_eg_mr3` has **no RUN-INDEX entry**. That matches my own record that this comparison is a tie at p=0.125 with a 0.65pp noise floor. A front-page ranking whose own supporting doc withdraws it is a bigger exposure than most of what a security review finds.

Also worth fixing: your local `entire-graph` checkout is on `114e178` from 07-28 and has **fully diverged** from `origin/main` — neither is an ancestor of the other.

I'll report the full audit — command execution, path traversal, symlinks, decompression, DoS, terminal injection, supply chain, secrets — when the finders and their adversarial verifiers land.

The security finders are still working (8 agents, 148K LOC). Meanwhile the catch-up analysis completed, and it produced a second verified bug.

## New: search results are printed out of score order on main

I reproduced this independently after my first attempt failed. The stable sort exists **only inside** `applyProseResolutionPromotions` (`search_multi_resolution.go:132`), but `expandProseResolution` early-returns at `len(results) >= topK` (`:165`). So whenever promotion doesn't run, nothing re-sorts, and blocks that append after ranking leave the array unordered.

The consequence for a consumer is direct: entire-graph tells agents these are ranked by relevance and to read the top hits first. A 0.45 above a 7.53 means the agent reads the wrong hits first — and it degrades silently, since nothing errors.

My first fixture missed it because every doc scored identically; the bug only surfaces once scores differ. Worth noting for whoever fixes it: a naive regression test will pass on tied scores.

## Your retrieval measurements survive

This was the thing I most wanted to know, and the answer is clean: **code-search ranking and payload are unchanged.** The finder built binaries at both `8f6764d` and `cceb4de` and got byte-identical JSON payloads on code-only repos at k=5/20/50. So last week's numbers — 55.6% first-payload gold-hit rate, calls-to-gold 5.64 vs baseline 4.79, the 0.980 substitution ratio — still describe current main. The one exception is docs-heavy mixed repos, where code results lose their `passages` field because passage planning is now path-gated.

What actually landed is that entire-graph became a **document retriever**, not just a code one: the prose ranked unit moved from file to section, so a 20-doc corpus can return 30 regions instead of being capped at 20, and multi-resolution promotion spends only slots the unit ranking left empty, bounded by `--max-context-bytes`.

## And a correction to one of my own long-standing findings

My "doctrine block was withheld" note had the wrong numbers. The shipped `agentGuide` is **2,497 bytes** and has not changed since 2026-07-30 — there is **no 1,908-byte guide anywhere** in the repo, at any commit. And the 893-byte artifact was never entire-graph's guide at all; it's graphmark's own harness-authored `tool_block.txt`. The substantive point stands and is actually sharper than I had it: **no benchmark cell ever delivered `agentGuide` in any size**, so the doctrine the product ships has never been tested. But my byte counts named two unrelated artifacts, and I should not have kept quoting them.

Two loose threads I'd flag while the audit finishes: `#88`'s cache **write** path is deliberately left unconfined (symlinked cache subdirs are tolerated by design — worth a look when the symlink finder reports), and `termsafe.Line` escapes TAB, so any one-line record carrying an interior tab now renders `\x09` — the exposed case being search type-card `Decl`.

content.text:
All 8 finders are still actively working (95–154 tool calls each) on the 148K LOC. The Workflow will notify me when they land. Meanwhile the catch-up synthesis produced one root cause and one correction I need to flag.

## The ordering bug I reproduced has a one-line root cause

`search_multi_resolution.go:165` gates promotion on `len(results) >= topK`, but `results` at that point **includes score-0 `related:sibling` locator rows** merged in at `search.go:1234`. Those aren't ranked hits. So the array looks full when it isn't, promotion silently never runs — and since the stable re-sort lives *inside* the promotion function, nothing re-sorts. One miscount produces both the missing promotions and the inversions I measured. The fix is to count only ranked entries and hoist the sort out of the promotion path.

The blast radius sits in a lane with **zero tests** for the configuration that matters: a docs-heavy repo that also contains source. That's precisely where section keying had silently uncapped `MaxRegionsPerFile` for `.go` files before `7ef28b9` caught it.

## My 893-byte finding is invalidated on both numbers — and the method was wrong

I've now had this corrected twice in one session, so let me state it properly. Re-measured on disk: eg `tool_block.txt` is **2,200–2,309 B**, baseline 470 B, cmm 1,596 B. No 893-byte block exists in any surviving graphmark cell. Worse for my methodology: **the size spread across eg cells is just the absolute checkout path repeated seven times.** I had been reading path-length noise as evidence of different instruction blocks.

What survives is the substantive half, and it's sharper than my version: **no benchmark cell ever delivered `agentGuide` at all**, in any size. The shipped guide is 2,497 B and unchanged since 07-30. The doctrine the product ships has never been benchmarked.

## My 28x cache number needs re-measuring

`#110` bumped both cache versions (`search-snapshot` v7→v8, `provider-records` v2→v3), which orphans every existing entry. The entries my `#92` fix newly made cacheable are the newest, so they lose the most. The 3704ms→131ms warm-repeat figure was measured on a pre-`#110` binary and no longer describes a fresh install's first run. Same caveat applies to the 7.9% wall-clock penalty.

## Where the security review stands

Still mid-flight. Confirmed so far, both independently reproduced by me:

- **`#90` shell injection was live and is correctly fixed** — repo-controlled VERIFY text reached `sh -c`, proven with `test_gizmo;touch PWNED_BY_VERIFY;.py`. Now POSIX-quoted at all ten interpolation sites. I checked `shellQuote` against `shlex.quote` and it's right.
- **`#96` termsafe closed a real terminal-spoofing primitive** — including the subtle case: `runeWidthAt` enforces UTF-8 well-formedness so an overlong `e0 80 9b` can't smuggle CSI inside a rune. A newline in a filename can no longer forge extra ranked-result lines.
- **`#88`/`#95` moved containment to `os.OpenRoot`** with nothing exploitable found today.
- **My `#92` gate is a reproduced silent-wrong-answer path**, still open on main.

The eight surfaces — command execution, path traversal, symlink/TOCTOU, decompression, ReDoS/DoS, output injection, supply chain, secrets/no-egress — each get an adversarial skeptic that defaults to REFUTED before anything reaches you. I'll report the triaged set with severities and CWEs when it completes.

input.command:
M=/Users/suhaan/.claude/projects/-Users-suhaan-devenv/memory
cat > $M/entire-graph-symlink-write-cwe59.md <<'EOF'
---
name: entire-graph-symlink-write-cwe59
description: "Two reproduced CWE-59 link-following writes in entire-graph main: init-agents appends and index --report TRUNCATES files outside the repo; root cause is os.Stat instead of os.Lstat"
metadata:
  type: project
---

2026-08-19, security review of entire-graph at cceb4de (origin/main). Two write primitives
REPRODUCED BY ME, not just agent-reported. Same root cause, same fix.

## 1. init-agents appends through a repo-controlled symlink  (CONFIRMED medium by adversarial verify)

```
internal/cli/agents.go:188  inspectInstructionFile uses os.Stat  <-- FOLLOWS the symlink
    if !info.Mode().IsRegular() { reject }                       <-- target IS regular -> passes
internal/cli/agents.go:148/153/177  os.WriteFile(...)            <-- follows link, writes target
```
`fileTypeName`'s `case mode&os.ModeSymlink != 0` (agents.go:208) is DEAD CODE: os.Stat never
returns a symlink mode, and a dangling link returns IsNotExist which is treated as the empty-file
case. The author wrote a symlink check that cannot fire.

Reproduced: hostile repo ships `AGENTS.md -> ../victim/dotfile.rc`; `entire graph init-agents`
(the documented onboarding command) printed "updated <repo>/AGENTS.md" and wrote the file OUTSIDE
the repo. Original content preserved + guide spliced in, so it is append/corrupt, not truncate.

## 2. index --report TRUNCATES through a repo-controlled symlink

```
internal/cli/index.go:129  os.WriteFile(flags.Report, ...)  no Lstat, no O_NOFOLLOW
```
Reproduced: `report.txt -> ../victim/precious.txt`, then `entire graph index --repo . --report
report.txt` -> "original data present: 0". FULL DATA DESTRUCTION of an arbitrary writable file.
Weaker trigger than #1 (the operator/wrapper supplies the --report path) but strictly worse impact,
and a CI job or agent wrapper choosing a repo-relative report path is natural.

## Threat model and severity

T1 malicious repo content. Victim clones a hostile repo (or checks out a PR branch) and runs a
documented command. Content written is the tool's own guide text, NOT attacker-chosen, so this is
an INTEGRITY/destruction bug, not RCE -- hence medium, not critical. Accepted class though:
CWE-59 / CWE-61 link-following, the git-symlink-checkout lineage.

**Fix:** `os.Lstat` in inspectInstructionFile (which makes the existing symlink branch live), and
for every os.WriteFile whose path can be repo-relative, open with O_NOFOLLOW|O_CREAT|O_EXCL or
Lstat-then-refuse. Audit all 71 file-write/read sites for the same pattern.

## Also from this review

- `#90` shell injection WAS live and IS correctly fixed: repo-derived VERIFY text reached
  `sh -c` (cli/verify.go:193); proven pre-fix with `test_gizmo;touch PWNED_BY_VERIFY;.py`.
  shellQuote matches shlex.quote exactly (allowlist `_@%+=:,./-`, `'` -> `'\''`); shellQuotePath
  prefixes `./` against option-shaped names. Sound.
- REFUTED by adversarial verify: unsigned release archives (needs contents:write already).
- Downgraded to low: git option injection CWE-88 at gitutil/git.go:380 (`diff --base/--head` bare
  args, 1 of 4 call sites missing the guard its siblings have); unguarded os.ReadFile of
  .graphignore in searchSnapshotKey; .gitignore negation defeating the .git exclusion
  (provider.go:10062); search emitting credential bytes with no secret deny-list.

**How to apply:** entire-graph writes files from repo-relative paths in at least two verbs with no
link guard. Before adding any new write, Lstat first. Related:
[[entire-graph-cache-gate-shebang-hole]].

print("indexed")
